north.ambientMood: Star-metal spires, cosmic absence, programmable lattices

south.name: The Crucible & Kinetic Foundry
south.ambientMood: Rust iron, kinetic gantries, orbital farm rings, sphere courses

east.ambientMood: Monolithic quartz blocks, data needles, private runtimes

west.ambientMood: Parchment monoliths, excavation trenches, historical foundations

infra.ambientMood: Heavy bus-bars, cooling columns, server monolithic pylons

sanctuary.name: Dexter Sanctuary
sanctuary.note: Deliberately outside project numbering, scoring, ranking, or semantic clustering.
sanctuary.description: A serene stone dais with a bronze lantern and a resting tricolor companion model, oriented towards the horizon. A fixed coordinate unaffected by semantic distortion.

projects.name: Starsilk Universe
projects.summary: A science-fantasy universe whose physics rest on Starsilk: a material that can be programmed like software.
projects.brief: Starsilk began as a question about what a world looks like if its fundamental material is programmable. The answer became a continuity-heavy universe with its own physics, factions, chronology and hard rules — Starsilk Macros, the Codec, the Shard-God Tiger, Syrin, the Drakken, the Administration, and the long consequence of the Starbinding. Its defining discipline is the separation of canon from invention: every addition is checked against what the setting has already committed to.
projects.lesson: A setting survives scale only when the rule that forbids something is written down as carefully as the thing it permits.

copy.subtitle: The Celestial Loom
copy.plaque: A universe whose physics are programmable. Pull one thread and the consequences propagate.
copy.problem: What does a world look like if its fundamental material behaves like software?
copy.made: A continuity-heavy science-fantasy universe with programmable Starsilk at its centre, held together by written rules about what canon forbids as much as what it permits.
copy.interaction: Pull the fundamental threads of the loom. Each change propagates visibly through the cosmological model above you.
copy.explore: Walk beneath the loom. The relationships between star nodes read differently from underneath than from the gallery floor.

projects.name: Drakken Terraforming Compendium
projects.summary: A thirty-seven entry field guide to the Drakken: one Egg, thirty-five strains across five archetypes, and one Mother.
projects.brief: The Compendium presents the Drakken the way a technical service manual presents machinery — as an in-universe forensic reference rather than a bestiary. Its structure is fixed at thirty-seven entries and its taxonomy at five archetypes, and its formatting doctrine (terminal-styled, stat-block driven) is treated as part of the canon rather than as decoration.
projects.lesson: A taxonomy is only useful if it describes a process; categories invented for tidiness fall apart the first time something has to be classified.

copy.subtitle: Thirty-seven Entries
copy.plaque: One Egg, thirty-five strains, one Mother. A terraforming taxonomy presented as a service manual.
copy.problem: How do you document a species that exists to perform an industrial process?
copy.made: A thirty-seven entry field compendium organised by five archetypes, with fixed formatting doctrine and a canon-correction record.
copy.interaction: Select a source-grounded process reference. The central Egg opens an abstract process glyph; it does not claim an undocumented specimen morphology.
copy.explore: Four canonical process references and one clearly marked taxonomy abstraction stand around the Egg. Mother is visible as a distant abstract relief.

projects.name: Orbital Tomb
projects.summary: A song, a narrative and an interactive tour about a station being taken apart in orbit over six months.
projects.brief: Orbital Tomb follows the Shard-God Tiger surgically dismantling Meridian Station in high orbit above Virgil. It exists simultaneously as music, as story, as visual production and as a browser-based Three.js tour, and each form was developed against the same six-month timeline rather than adapted from one another after the fact.
projects.lesson: When several media share one timeline instead of one script, they stop being adaptations of each other and start being views of the same event.

copy.subtitle: Six Months Over Virgil
copy.plaque: Not an explosion — a dismantling, carried out with intent across six months.
copy.problem: How do you tell one event as a song, a story, a visual production and an interactive tour without any of them becoming an adaptation?
copy.made: A Starsilk production in four simultaneous media, all developed against a single six-month dismantling timeline.
copy.interaction: Turn the dismantling dial. The station segment reconfigures from Month Zero through Month Six.
copy.explore: Enter the station fragment. The interior changes with the dial.

projects.name: Starsilk Possibility Cartographer
projects.summary: A deterministic engine that maps what canon has used, forbidden, contradicted, left unresolved, and still permits.
projects.brief: The Cartographer treats a fictional canon as a body of evidence rather than a pile of text. It indexes sources, assigns epistemic states to claims, runs ontology checks, and produces a map of negative space: the regions a setting has not yet spent. It runs entirely locally and produces the same answer for the same snapshot every time.
projects.lesson: A tool that maps what is still possible is more useful than one that generates possibilities, because the first one can be argued with.

copy.subtitle: Mapping Negative Space
copy.plaque: A canon is not only what it has said. It is also what it has forbidden, contradicted, and left open.
copy.problem: How do you know what a fictional universe still permits you to invent?
copy.made: A deterministic local engine that assigns evidence states to canon claims and maps the possibility space that remains legal.
copy.interaction: Select a canon fact. Legal possibilities illuminate, contradictions close, and unresolved regions stay dark — because absence of a rule is not permission.
copy.explore: The possibility graph is volumetric. Walk into it and inspect relationships from inside the structure.

projects.name: StarSilk Maker
projects.summary: A generative instrument that turns drawn paths into woven Starsilk compositions.
projects.brief: StarSilk Maker is the setting's central material made operable. A path becomes a thread; threads accumulate into a composition governed by the same weaving rules the universe describes. It is the project where Starsilk stopped being a description and became something a person could actually manipulate.
projects.lesson: The fastest way to find out whether an invented material has coherent rules is to build something that has to obey them.

copy.subtitle: Weaving the Material
copy.plaque: The moment the setting's central material stopped being a description and became something you could hold.
copy.problem: Does the invented material actually have coherent rules, or only convincing ones?
copy.made: A generative instrument that turns drawn paths into woven Starsilk compositions obeying the canon rules for tension and interference.
copy.interaction: Draw a path through the air above the loom. The mechanism weaves it into a thread composition.
copy.explore: Completed fibres extend outward from the loom as a small sculpture that persists while you are in the room.

projects.name: Drakken Field Anatomy Archive
projects.status: Experimental; not implemented in the inspected baseline
projects.summary: A forensic anatomy reference separating canon Drakken specimens from deliberately non-canon surrogates.
projects.brief: The Anatomy Archive documents Drakken internal structure at four levels — external form, skeletal frame, energy and process systems, and cross-section. Its most important structural decision is a hard separation between canon specimens and intentionally non-canon surrogate specimens used for teaching, so that illustrative material can never be mistaken for canon.
projects.lesson: Teaching material and canon material must be labelled differently at the point of creation, not at the point of publication.

copy.subtitle: Four Layers Down
copy.plaque: Drakken organs are stages of a process. The anatomy is a pipeline diagram.
copy.problem: How do you teach the structure of a creature without teaching things canon never established?
copy.made: A forensic anatomy reference with four view layers and a hard separation between canon specimens and deliberately non-canon teaching surrogates.
copy.interaction: Cycle each table through external, skeletal, energy-process and section views.
copy.explore: Three tables stand side by side. The surrogate specimen is marked and separated — the marking is part of the exhibit.

projects.name: The Drakken Terraforming Laboratory
projects.summary: A simulation of the Drakken terraforming pipeline, from raw collection through to breathable sky.
projects.brief: The Laboratory runs the process the Compendium describes. Drakken strains are deployed against a hostile world and their functions chain together: Gorevault collection, gathering, rendering and refinement produce feedstock; Ringthroat converts feedstock into SKY. The world visibly changes as the chain runs.
projects.lesson: Writing a process down proves it is describable; running it proves it is coherent. They are not the same test.

copy.subtitle: The Process Lock
copy.plaque: Gorevault gathers and refines. Ringthroat makes sky. Collapse the two and the world stops changing.
copy.problem: Is the terraforming process described in the Compendium actually coherent, or only plausible?
copy.made: A deterministic simulation of the full Drakken pipeline: collection, gathering, rendering and refinement into feedstock, then feedstock into SKY.
copy.interaction: Deploy strains against the world above the engineering floor. The pipeline executes in order and the planet visibly changes.
copy.explore: Walk the full circle of the engineering floor. The world transforms differently depending on which side you watch from.

projects.name: Heliocide Observatory
projects.status: Active; prototype validated in repository evidence
projects.summary: An observatory for watching the Heliocide: stars going out, one after another, in the correct order.
projects.brief: The Observatory reconstructs the extinguishing of stars across the setting's sky. Its hardest requirement is a visual rule: from an inhabited world, the Siege Wall must read as an absence — a swath of sky where stars are simply no longer there — and never as masonry, lattice or grid.
projects.lesson: Some canon rules are about what a thing must not look like; those are the ones that get violated most often and matter most.

copy.subtitle: The Siege Wall Is an Absence
copy.plaque: From an inhabited world the Siege Wall is not a structure. It is the shape of what has been removed.
copy.problem: How do you render the extinguishing of a sky without turning an absence into an object?
copy.made: An observatory that plays back stellar extinction in canon order, under a hard visual rule forbidding any masonry, lattice or grid reading.
copy.interaction: Begin the reconstruction. Stars leave the sky in the order canon requires.
copy.explore: Three telescope stations give genuinely different views of the same event. The difference is the point.

projects.name: Museum of Me / The Reliquary of Iterative Becoming
projects.summary: The earlier attempts to build this museum, preserved as evidence rather than hidden.
projects.brief: Before this building existed there were several Museum of Me concepts, including a large single-file Three.js artifact titled The Reliquary of Iterative Becoming. Those artifacts remain intact as historical evidence. This building is a separate lineage — a new collection structure, asset pipeline and production contract — rather than another restoration pass over the old one.
projects.lesson: There is a point where restoring an artifact costs more than rebuilding the thing it was trying to be.

copy.subtitle: The Building Before This One
copy.plaque: Earlier attempts at this museum, preserved rather than hidden — including the one that proved a single file could not hold it.
copy.problem: Is this museum a restoration of the previous artifact, or a new lineage?
copy.made: A record of the Museum of Me and Reliquary concepts, the large single-file Three.js artifact they produced, and the decision to build this version as a separate product.
copy.interaction: Turn the timeline control. Earlier museum concepts rise from the maquette table as layered models.
copy.explore: The final layer is the building you are standing in.

projects.name: WorldsVault Uplink
projects.summary: The first and most ambitious attempt at a worldbuilding and canon-management platform.
projects.brief: Uplink was the research phase: a broad architecture study for a platform that would hold canon, relationships, technology reports and product structure in one system. It produced substantial architecture and technology analysis and very little running software, and it was superseded rather than abandoned.
projects.lesson: Architecture research is not wasted when the architecture is rejected — but it is wasted if nothing is ever narrowed.

projects.name: CanonForge
projects.summary: The narrowing: a Markdown vault, a Python CLI, schemas, validation and transfer packets.
projects.brief: CanonForge cut the platform ambition down to something that could run on one machine. Canon lives as Markdown, structure lives in schemas, correctness is enforced by validation, and knowledge moves between contexts as explicit transfer packets. A later interface layer was considered but the command line remained the honest surface.
projects.lesson: Narrowing an ambitious system to one machine and plain files is usually the step that makes it real.

projects.name: WorldsVault
projects.summary: The surviving form: an Obsidian and Git vault for canon, workflows and technical knowledge, with local retrieval.
projects.brief: WorldsVault is what the lineage settled into. Canon, workflow notes and technical knowledge live in an Obsidian vault under Git, retrieval runs locally against local models, and handoffs to other tools are explicit artifacts. It kept CanonForge's file-first discipline and dropped the requirement to build a bespoke application around it.
projects.lesson: Three generations of the same idea, each smaller than the last, and the smallest one is the one still running.

copy.subtitle: Three Generations, Each Smaller
copy.plaque: A platform became a command-line tool became a folder of Markdown. The folder is the one still running.
copy.problem: What is the smallest system that can hold a body of canon for years?
copy.made: Three successive canon-management systems: a platform architecture study, a local-first tool with schemas and transfer packets, and finally a versioned vault of plain files.
copy.interaction: Feed the same lore record into each machine in turn and watch how its representation — and the machinery required — changes.
copy.explore: The three machines are connected in sequence. Each is visibly simpler than the one before it.

projects.name: KinDex Handoff
projects.summary: A handoff builder that stages evidence-linked claims for human approval before they become project record.
projects.brief: KinDex scans project material and proposes claims about it — what exists, what state it is in, what remains. Every claim carries a link back to the evidence that produced it, and nothing enters the record until a person approves it. Its outputs are handoff documents, task lists, open questions, a source index and an append-only project record.
projects.lesson: Automated project summaries need a human approval step, because a plausible wrong claim is more expensive than no claim.

projects.name: ChatGPT Bible Repo
projects.summary: A Git repository that holds project identity and history so it survives outside any single conversation.
projects.brief: The Bible Repo is where project continuity actually lives. Each project has an append-only record of its identity, decisions, handoffs and recognition metadata, stored in Git so that a new conversation in any tool can be brought up to speed from evidence rather than from memory.
projects.lesson: Context that lives only in a conversation is context you are going to lose.

projects.name: Project Forge
projects.summary: A progress tracker for long-horizon work, built around lifecycle stages rather than task lists.
projects.brief: Project Forge tracks creative, business, software and experimental work over years rather than sprints. It models lifecycle stages, recurring rituals, releases and capture, with progression mechanics layered on top. An artifact was built; which build is canonical was never firmly established.
projects.lesson: A tool for tracking long projects has to survive the same neglect it is designed to detect.

copy.subtitle: Context That Survives the Conversation
copy.plaque: Project context that lives only in a conversation is project context you are going to lose.
copy.problem: How does a project remember itself across tools, sessions and years?
copy.made: A handoff builder with an approval gate, an append-only project record in version control, and a long-horizon progress tracker.
copy.interaction: Assemble a handoff from evidence blocks. Claims without supporting evidence are rejected by the mechanism.
copy.explore: The documentation chain runs the length of the alcove; each stage physically refuses input the previous stage did not justify.

projects.name: Rhetorical InDEX
projects.summary: An offline tool that separates a statement's evidence from its interpretation, framing and inference.
projects.brief: Rhetorical InDEX takes a piece of writing apart into the moves it is making. A sentence can assert evidence, interpret evidence, frame a topic, draw an inference, or claim something with no support at all — and readers routinely fail to notice which is which. The prototype shipped as a single offline file with no network dependency.
projects.lesson: The useful question about a claim is rarely whether it is true; it is which kind of claim it is.

copy.subtitle: Which Kind of Claim Is This?
copy.plaque: The useful question about a statement is rarely whether it is true. It is what kind of move it is making.
copy.problem: Readers fail to notice when a text shifts from reporting evidence to framing it.
copy.made: An offline single-file analysis tool that classifies spans of writing as evidence, interpretation, framing, inference or unsupported claim.
copy.interaction: Sort sample statements into the five categories on the evidence table. The table shows the classification the tool would assign, and why.
copy.explore: All examples here are invented. No real dispute, publication or person is analysed in this room.

projects.name: Suno AI Lyrics and Manual
projects.summary: A working manual for songwriting with a generative music model, built from what actually reproduced.
projects.brief: This project is a codex rather than an application: a durable body of doctrine covering lyric structure, narration, style prompts and parameter behaviour for Suno V5. It was assembled by writing songs, observing which instructions changed the output and which were ignored, and recording only the parts that held up across attempts.
projects.lesson: A prompt manual is only worth keeping if it records the techniques that failed alongside the ones that worked.

copy.subtitle: What Actually Reproduced
copy.plaque: A prompt manual worth keeping records the techniques that failed alongside the ones that worked.
copy.problem: Which instructions to a generative music model actually change the output, and which are ignored?
copy.made: A durable songwriting codex covering lyric structure, narration, style-prompt grammar and parameter behaviour, assembled from repeated testing.
copy.interaction: Switch between original project excerpts at the desk and raise or lower the simplified arrangement layers.
copy.explore: Instrument and waveform objects in the room respond spatially to whatever is currently playing.

projects.name: Visual Prompt Systems Registry
projects.summary: A registry of image-prompt templates with batch syntax, categories and explicit negative constraints.
projects.brief: The Registry treats visual prompts as reusable components instead of one-off text. Templates carry slots, categories organise them, dynamic batch syntax expands one template into a controlled set of variations, and negative constraints are stored with the template rather than remembered separately.
projects.lesson: The reusable part of a prompt is usually the constraint list, not the description.

projects.name: Vibe Coding Nexus / DexGate Academy
projects.summary: A game-like learning environment for people building software with AI tools for the first time.
projects.brief: DexGate Academy teaches the practice of building software conversationally — choosing tools, structuring a project, recognising when progress has stalled — to an audience that does not already have programming habits. It is delivered as an interactive, beginner-safe experience rather than as documentation.
projects.lesson: Teaching people to build software with AI is mostly teaching them to recognise when the conversation has stopped making progress.

copy.subtitle: Prompts as Components
copy.plaque: The reusable part of a prompt is usually the constraint list, not the description.
copy.problem: Generative prompts are rewritten from scratch every time, and their hard-won negative constraints are lost first.
copy.made: A registry of visual-prompt templates with batch syntax and stored negative constraints, and a beginner-safe environment for learning to build software conversationally.
copy.interaction: Combine deterministic prompt blocks in the assembly machine. The rendered scene beyond the glass changes to match — no external service involved.
copy.explore: Constraint blocks are physically different from description blocks, and the machine will not run without them.

projects.name: Code Harness
projects.summary: An orchestration layer that routes work between reusable workflows, local inference and specialist agents.
projects.brief: Code Harness assembles the working parts of an AI development setup into one addressable system: reusable workflows, project context, local model inference, specialist agent definitions, and the handoff artifacts that move work between them. Its persistence lives in the Bible Repo rather than in the harness itself.
projects.lesson: Orchestration systems should not own the memory they orchestrate, or they become impossible to replace.

projects.name: Opencode Harness
projects.summary: An attempt to make several different coding agents share one context and hand work to each other.
projects.brief: Opencode Harness explored interoperability between separate agent tools — OpenCode, Claude Code and a local coding agent — with shared context, common orchestration and a handoff format that survived the boundary between them. It is local-first and currently paused.
projects.lesson: Integrating fast-moving tools costs more than the integration saves until the tools slow down.

copy.subtitle: Routing the Work
copy.plaque: An orchestration system should not own the memory it orchestrates, or it becomes impossible to replace.
copy.problem: How do several different AI development tools share one project's context and hand work to each other?
copy.made: Two orchestration harnesses: one assembling workflows, context and specialist agents around durable external persistence, one attempting interoperability between separate coding agents.
copy.interaction: Route a task through the rack: request, context assembly, specialist selection, validation, handoff.
copy.explore: Persistence sits outside the rack, physically separate, connected by a single cable.

projects.name: Guy_Cast
projects.summary: The first generation: a desktop application plus browser extension for casting media.
projects.brief: Guy_Cast spanned a Tauri desktop application, a web surface and a Chrome extension, all covering the same media-casting workflow. Supporting three delivery targets for one feature set proved to be the project's defining cost, and its successor chose a single native platform instead.
projects.lesson: Shipping one feature to three platforms at once triples the maintenance before it doubles the audience.

projects.name: Gay_Cast
projects.summary: The successor: one native Android application instead of three cross-platform surfaces.
projects.brief: Gay_Cast rebuilt the casting workflow as a native Android application in Kotlin and Jetpack Compose. Dropping to a single platform removed the multi-surface maintenance cost that stalled its predecessor and let the feature set develop instead of merely being ported.
projects.lesson: The second generation is usually smaller in scope and larger in capability than the first.

projects.name: He-Maker
projects.summary: A creative application recovered from cloud storage and rebuilt into a durable repository.
projects.brief: He-Maker existed as a folder in cloud storage before it existed as a project. Its recovery — reconstructing the source into a repository with a written project record — is the work that made it a project again rather than an archive of files.
projects.lesson: Files in a sync folder are a backup, not a project; the difference is history and stated intent.

projects.name: Media Getter
projects.summary: A macOS utility that downloads, converts, trims and transcribes media using bundled command-line tools.
projects.brief: Media Getter puts a native interface over a set of command-line media tools and bundles them so the application works without the user installing anything. Its lineage split when a separate reimplementation was attempted alongside the original.
projects.lesson: A utility that wraps command-line tools should ship them; otherwise the wrapper inherits every installation problem it was meant to hide.

copy.subtitle: Four Generations of the Same Idea
copy.plaque: One feature shipped to three platforms triples the maintenance before it doubles the audience.
copy.problem: A media workflow was rebuilt repeatedly as the delivery strategy changed underneath it.
copy.made: A cross-platform casting application, its native Android successor, a recovered creative application, and a native media utility with bundled tooling.
copy.interaction: Run a media workflow across the bench: input, trim, convert, transcribe, output. Each device generation handles the same job differently.
copy.explore: The devices are arranged chronologically. Each is smaller in scope than the one before it.

projects.name: DexDictate macOS
projects.summary: System-wide dictation for macOS that runs entirely on the machine, with no speech leaving it.
projects.brief: DexDictate is a menu-bar application that transcribes speech into whatever text field currently has focus, anywhere in the operating system. Recognition runs locally through a bundled Whisper implementation, so dictation works offline and no audio is transmitted.
projects.lesson: Concurrency bugs in audio code do not show up in testing; they show up in the third minute of real dictation.

projects.name: DexDictate Android
projects.summary: The same idea on Android, rebuilt as an input method rather than ported.
projects.brief: On Android, system-wide text entry is an input method — a keyboard the operating system installs — not an accessibility overlay. DexDictate Android is therefore a separate implementation of the same intent, informed by the macOS product's behaviour but sharing none of its mechanism.
projects.lesson: Cross-platform products share intent, not implementation; treating the second platform as a port hides the real work.

projects.name: DexSpeak
projects.summary: A macOS text-to-speech application with multiple synthesis backends behind one interface.
projects.brief: DexSpeak reads text aloud using whichever synthesis engine suits the request — system voices for speed, neural backends for quality, custom voices where they exist. The provider architecture that hides this choice from the interface is its most durable contribution.
projects.lesson: When several engines do the same job badly in different ways, the abstraction over them is the actual product.

projects.name: DexTalk
projects.summary: A voice-cloning workbench forked from DexSpeak's interface so the original could stay untouched.
projects.brief: DexTalk is a local Python and Gradio laboratory for voice cloning. It deliberately reimplements the DexSpeak interface rather than extending it, so that experimental work could proceed without putting a working application at risk.
projects.lesson: Forking a working tool to run experiments costs a little duplication and saves the working tool.

projects.name: BigMac Voice Tools
projects.summary: A laptop control surface for voice models that run on a much larger machine elsewhere on the network.
projects.brief: Voice synthesis and cloning are expensive. BigMac Voice Tools keeps the models on a dedicated machine and gives the laptop a control interface and a transfer path, so the light device drives the work without attempting to do it.
projects.lesson: Deciding which machine does the work is an architecture decision, not a deployment detail.

copy.subtitle: Speech That Never Leaves the Machine
copy.plaque: Five voice projects, one requirement: recognition and synthesis run locally, and audio is not transmitted.
copy.problem: Dictation and voice synthesis are useful everywhere and trustworthy almost nowhere.
copy.made: System-wide macOS dictation with local recognition, a separate Android input method, a multi-provider synthesis application, a voice-cloning fork, and a thin client for models running on a larger machine.
copy.interaction: Select a prerecorded sample and compare raw transcription, refined transcription, synthesised voice and command interpretation at the four stations.
copy.explore: No microphone permission is requested. Every sample in this room is prerecorded.

projects.name: DexGPT / DnDex Operating Project
projects.summary: A working context that governs how an assistant behaves across sessions: voice, memory, exactness.
projects.brief: DexGPT is a persona and continuity system — a set of rules about voice, memory handling, project continuity and how precisely an instruction must be followed. It is named after Dexter and shaped by him, but it is software, and this museum keeps that distinction strictly.
projects.lesson: A useful assistant configuration is mostly a list of things it must not silently decide for you.

projects.name: DexClawdBot / Clawdbot
projects.summary: A local assistant with append-only memory the user could inspect, correct, pin or forget.
projects.brief: Clawdbot reached the user through a messaging transport and kept its memory as an append-only stream with provenance attached to every entry. The controls it exposed — inspect, correct, pin, forget — are the part worth preserving, and the project is defunct.
projects.lesson: An assistant's memory needs a forget button that leaves a mark, not one that pretends nothing was there.

projects.name: DexKeeper Bot
projects.summary: A single-community moderation bot that installs like a normal application and stores everything locally.
projects.brief: DexKeeper moderates one community. It polls rather than requiring an inbound webhook, keeps its state in a local database, and installs natively on Windows, macOS and Linux without a container runtime — decisions that make it deployable by someone who runs a community rather than a server.
projects.lesson: Self-hosted software fails at installation far more often than at runtime.

copy.subtitle: Software Shaped by a Dog
copy.plaque: These are systems named after Dexter. Dexter himself is elsewhere in this building, and the distinction is deliberate.
copy.problem: An assistant that forgets its own rules between sessions cannot be relied on for anything exacting.
copy.made: A persona and continuity system governing voice and exactness, a local assistant with inspectable append-only memory, and a self-hosted community moderation bot.
copy.interaction: Route a request among the agent roles and watch which memory each one is permitted to read and write.
copy.explore: The memory column is append-only: entries can be pinned or marked forgotten, but the mark itself remains visible.

projects.name: DexTilt
projects.summary: Turning a phone's motion into authenticated commands on a desktop machine.
projects.brief: DexTilt pairs an Android phone with a Mac receiver and converts physical gestures — tilt, rotation, motion — into commands from a fixed allowlist. Pairing happens by QR code, gestures are trained rather than hardcoded, and manual controls exist for everything the motion path can do.
projects.lesson: A novel input method needs a boring fallback, or it becomes a novelty that gets uninstalled.

copy.subtitle: Motion as Command
copy.plaque: A novel input method needs a boring fallback, or it becomes a novelty that gets uninstalled.
copy.problem: Can physical gestures with a phone safely drive a desktop machine?
copy.made: A paired phone-and-desktop bridge converting trained motion gestures into commands from an explicit allowlist, with manual equivalents for everything.
copy.interaction: Take hold of the phone model and tilt it. The desktop station responds to the gesture events in real time.
copy.explore: Your gesture trajectories remain in the air as visible spatial ribbons until they fade.

projects.name: DexCleaner
projects.summary: A disk cleanup tool built around reversibility and approval rather than automatic deletion.
projects.brief: DexCleaner audits disk usage and proposes cleanups. Nothing is removed without explicit approval and the design favours reversible operations, because the category of tool it belongs to has a long history of deleting things people wanted.
projects.lesson: In destructive tooling, the features you decline to build are as much a part of the design as the ones you ship.

projects.name: DexSort
projects.summary: Image sorting where the device stays the archive and nothing is uploaded or destroyed.
projects.brief: DexSort organises a large image collection on an Android tablet under two hard rules: the tablet remains the authoritative archive, and no operation may destroy an original or send it to a cloud service. Sorting is therefore organisational, never lossy.
projects.lesson: Stating the prohibitions before the features produces a smaller and more trustworthy application.

projects.name: SpaceWise
projects.summary: An Android storage explainer that refuses to overclaim what deleting something will do.
projects.brief: SpaceWise makes device storage understandable — what is using space, why, and what would change if it were removed. It is deliberately built against the norms of its category: it does not promise recovered gigabytes, does not claim to make a device faster, and does not silently involve cloud storage.
projects.lesson: In a category built on exaggeration, accuracy is a feature users can feel.

copy.subtitle: What the Tool Declines to Do
copy.plaque: In destructive tooling, the features you refuse to build are as much of the design as the ones you ship.
copy.problem: Storage and cleanup utilities have a long history of deleting things people wanted and overstating what they recovered.
copy.made: A reversible approval-gated macOS disk auditor, a non-destructive on-device image sorter, and an Android storage explainer that refuses to overclaim.
copy.interaction: Sort synthetic files across the bench. Destructive operations are physically unavailable — the mechanism has no such lever.
copy.explore: Every file on this bench is synthetic. The exhibit has no access to any real filesystem.

projects.name: DexAid
projects.summary: A local casefile tool for navigating institutions during an emergency, built around chronology and evidence.
projects.brief: DexAid helps a person in a stabilisation crisis — housing, benefits, utilities, medical administration, banking, insurance — assemble what institutions actually require: an accurate chronology, the evidence supporting it, and a defensible next action. Everything stays on the user's machine.
projects.lesson: Software for a crisis has to produce the artifact the institution asks for, not a better internal representation of the problem.

projects.name: DexEnhance
projects.summary: A browser extension that improves AI chat interfaces without touching the pages it sits on.
projects.brief: DexEnhance adds workflow improvements to ChatGPT and Gemini from inside the browser. Its interface renders in Shadow DOM so it cannot collide with the host page's styles, and its storage is local-first so nothing it records leaves the browser.
projects.lesson: An extension that styles itself inside the host page is a maintenance contract with someone else's redesign schedule.

copy.subtitle: The Artifact the Institution Asks For
copy.plaque: Software for a crisis has to produce what the institution requires, not a better internal model of the problem.
copy.problem: Institutional processes fail people who cannot produce an accurate chronology with evidence attached.
copy.made: A local-first emergency casefile application for housing, benefits, utilities and medical administration, and a browser extension improving AI workflow surfaces.
copy.interaction: Using an entirely fictional situation, assemble a chronology, attach evidence to each event, and produce a next-action packet.
copy.explore: The situation on this table is invented. No real case record, correspondence or personal document appears in this museum.

projects.name: DexCraft
projects.summary: A menu-bar tool that rewrites rough text into a structured prompt shaped for a specific target.
projects.brief: DexCraft takes an unstructured idea and produces a prompt formatted for a particular destination — a chat assistant, a research tool, an agentic development environment — because these targets reward genuinely different structures. It runs offline and lives in the menu bar so it is available mid-task.
projects.lesson: Prompt structure is target-dependent; a universal prompt formatter is a formatter for nothing in particular.

projects.name: DexGen
projects.summary: Image generation on borrowed hardware, with results persisted somewhere they will survive the session.
projects.brief: DexGen runs image generation on hosted notebook infrastructure, exposes it through a key-protected inference API, persists generated files to durable storage, and reaches the outside through a temporary tunnel. It is the pragmatic answer to needing a GPU that the local machines do not have.
projects.lesson: Ephemeral compute is only useful once you have solved where the output goes.

projects.name: DexDraw
projects.summary: A collaborative drawing surface rebuilt several times, each generation keeping less of the last.
projects.brief: DexDraw is a shared whiteboard and drawing application with an unusually visible lineage: an original, a redux, and a vNext redesign, each a substantial rewrite rather than an iteration. The lineage itself is instructive about how collaborative-editing requirements reshape an architecture.
projects.lesson: Some requirements cannot be retrofitted; you find out by trying, and the attempt is the education.

copy.subtitle: Making Things That Make Things
copy.plaque: Three creative tools whose lineages show the same lesson: some requirements cannot be retrofitted.
copy.problem: Creative tools accumulate requirements — collaboration, offline operation, target-specific output — that reshape their architecture rather than extending it.
copy.made: An offline prompt-shaping menu-bar application, a hosted image-generation service with durable persistence, and a collaborative whiteboard rebuilt across three generations.
copy.interaction: Draw directly on the design table. Your marks appear on its surface and connect into the shared composition.
copy.explore: The table surface is a live drawing texture. What visitors draw persists for the length of your visit.

projects.name: DexEarth
projects.summary: A tactical globe that layers flights, satellites, earthquakes, fires, cables and tectonics into one view.
projects.brief: DexEarth is a CesiumJS and React globe that composes many independent geospatial feeds into a single navigable surface, then looks for correlations between them. It supports simulations, alerts, derived threat indices and several render styles.
projects.lesson: Combining ordinary data layers produces genuinely new questions; the composition is the contribution.
capabilities: Flights, satellites, seismic, fire, cable and tectonic layers

projects.name: Dexterpreter
projects.summary: Spanish speech transcription and English translation running entirely in the browser, offline.
projects.brief: Dexterpreter listens to Spanish speech, transcribes it and translates it into English with models that run in the browser through Transformers.js. Nothing is sent to a service, which makes it usable in exactly the situations — medical, legal, institutional — where a cloud translator is inappropriate.
projects.lesson: For sensitive conversations, an offline translator that is somewhat less accurate is the more useful tool.

copy.subtitle: Composition and Boundary
copy.plaque: Combining ordinary data layers produces genuinely new questions. The composition is the contribution.
copy.problem: Geospatial and language tools are individually common and rarely combined or made private.
copy.made: A tactical globe layering flights, satellites, seismic events, fires, undersea cables and tectonics into one correlatable view, and an offline in-browser speech translator.
copy.interaction: Choose a location on the globe and raise the layers. At the language wall, run a controlled translation example — entirely offline.
copy.explore: No live map service is contacted. Every layer and translation here is bundled sample data.

projects.name: Era of Invincible Magic: Lands Unknown
projects.summary: A full campaign for Battle for Wesnoth, authored data-first with its own architect workflow.
projects.brief: Lands Unknown is a campaign and sourcebook for Battle for Wesnoth 1.18. Its distinguishing decision is that the campaign was authored as structured data — units, identifiers, dialogue, mechanics, scenario definitions — before it was authored as content, using a purpose-built workflow to keep the two consistent.
projects.lesson: Content-heavy game projects are database problems wearing a narrative costume.

copy.subtitle: A Campaign as a Database
copy.plaque: Content-heavy game projects are database problems wearing a narrative costume.
copy.problem: A campaign of this size collapses when the same unit is referenced three different ways in three different files.
copy.made: A complete campaign and sourcebook for a strategy game, authored data-first with a purpose-built workflow keeping identifiers, dialogue and mechanics consistent.
copy.interaction: Select regions and artifacts on the campaign table. Terrain rises and campaign paths respond.
copy.explore: Miniature environments lift out of the map surface as you select their regions.

projects.name: DnDex / DM_Hub
projects.summary: An encounter runner for a game master: initiative, hit points, a tactical map, and nothing that slows the table.
projects.brief: DnDex is a local D&D 5e encounter-management application built around the reality that a game master is doing several things at once under time pressure. Initiative order, hit-point tracking, a tactical map, a bestiary and rules reference sit in one workspace with persistence, history and import/export.
projects.lesson: Tools used under time pressure are judged on interaction cost, not on feature count.

copy.subtitle: Tools Used Under Pressure
copy.plaque: A tool used at a table is judged on interaction cost, not on feature count.
copy.problem: A game master is tracking initiative, hit points, positions and rules simultaneously while people wait.
copy.made: A local encounter-management application with initiative order, hit-point control, a tactical map, bestiary, rules reference, persistence and history.
copy.interaction: Run a single deterministic encounter round: roll, adjust initiative, move a miniature, resolve one action.
copy.explore: The table is small and complete. It is not a D&D engine and does not pretend to be.

projects.name: WESTCAT Overlay
projects.summary: A long-running family of translucent always-on-top desktop overlays for live production.
projects.brief: The WESTCAT overlays are broadcast-facing desktop windows: translucent, always on top, click-through when needed, with persistent settings, polling, player controls and a cat-and-speech-bubble presentation. The family spans many repositories because each production need produced another variant.
projects.lesson: Tools built under live production deadlines fragment into variants, because there is never a moment to consolidate them.

projects.name: WestCat Goes East
projects.summary: A 16-bit-styled platformer set in a real place, with a generated asset pipeline behind it.
projects.brief: WestCat Goes East is an HTML5 Canvas platformer in the visual idiom of the 16-bit era, set around a recognisable stretch of Vancouver Island and starring the WestCat characters. A substantial generated asset-pack workflow supplies its sprites and tiles.
projects.lesson: In a generated-art project the consistency pipeline is the project; individual assets are the easy part.

copy.subtitle: Built to a Live Deadline
copy.plaque: Tools built under live production deadlines fragment into variants, because there is never a moment to consolidate them.
copy.problem: Broadcast overlays must sit on top of everything, be readable, and never obstruct the thing they annotate.
copy.made: A long-running family of translucent always-on-top desktop overlays with click-through modes and producer-safe controls, and a 16-bit-styled platformer set in real geography.
copy.interaction: Toggle overlay layers and routes on the operations map. Each layer can be made click-through, exactly as in production.
copy.explore: The fragmented repository lineage is shown honestly: the variants are the artifact.

projects.name: The Full Weasel
projects.summary: A finished birthday rhythm game in which Dexter catches treats and dodges sharks.
projects.brief: The Full Weasel is a mobile-first rhythm game made as a birthday gift. Dexter catches falling treats in time with the music, avoids sharks, fills a party meter and reaches an escalating celebratory finale. It is small, complete and playable — which makes it rare in this collection.
projects.lesson: A hard external deadline is the most reliable scope-control mechanism there is.

copy.subtitle: Finished
copy.plaque: Among sixty-four projects, this one is complete and playable. A hard deadline did what deadlines do.
copy.problem: Scope grows until something external stops it.
copy.made: A mobile-first rhythm game made as a birthday gift, in which Dexter catches treats, avoids sharks and fills a party meter toward a celebratory finale.
copy.interaction: Three linked mechanisms in the cabinet, each escalating the result of the last.
copy.explore: Small footprint, strong personality. The cabinet takes up less space than most cases in this wing.

projects.name: Against the Void
projects.summary: A station survival and defence game built in Godot, with unusually heavy interface work.
projects.brief: Against the Void combines survival, management and defence aboard a station under threat. Most of its engineering went into interface and interaction — a management game is almost entirely interface — alongside packaging and repeated systematic bug sweeps.
projects.lesson: In management games the interface is not the presentation layer; it is the game.

copy.subtitle: The Interface Is the Game
copy.plaque: In management games the interface is not the presentation layer. It is the entire mechanism.
copy.problem: A player must read threat, resources and options at a glance without the screen becoming noise.
copy.made: A station survival, management and defence game with extensive interface engineering, packaging and repeated systematic bug sweeps.
copy.interaction: Place fleet pieces on the tactical star table and resolve one deterministic combat turn.
copy.explore: The table reads from any side; information density was the design problem.

projects.name: Arkship Civilization
projects.summary: A civilization-scale generation-ship project, scoped down to one falsifiable prototype.
projects.brief: Arkship Civilization is a generation-ship simulation whose entire preproduction is organised around a single prototype called The Descent Decision — ninety to a hundred and twenty minutes long, built to answer whether the core idea is actually interesting before anything larger is committed.
projects.lesson: A prototype that cannot fail is not a prototype; it is a demo.

copy.subtitle: The Descent Decision
copy.plaque: A prototype that cannot fail is not a prototype. It is a demo.
copy.problem: Is a civilization-scale generation-ship game actually interesting, or only impressive to describe?
copy.made: A modular arkship simulation scoped entirely around one falsifiable hundred-minute prototype built to answer that question before anything larger was committed.
copy.interaction: Explode the ship into its modules — command, habitation, logistics, energy, propulsion — then choose a destination and watch one module deploy.
copy.explore: The ship hangs at full length above the gallery. Walk its axis to read the module sequence.

projects.name: AetherVFX
projects.summary: A browser workbench for building procedural visual effects with live parameter control.
projects.brief: AetherVFX is a Three.js environment for authoring ability and procedural effects: emitters, forces, lifetimes, turbulence and colour behaviour are exposed as live controls so an effect is shaped by watching it rather than by editing and reloading.
projects.lesson: Any authoring tool for something judged by eye must close the feedback loop to zero.

copy.subtitle: Zero Feedback Delay
copy.plaque: Any authoring tool for something judged by eye must close the feedback loop to nothing.
copy.problem: Visual effects are tuned by watching them, and every second between change and result degrades the result.
copy.made: A browser workbench for procedural ability effects with live control over emitters, forces, lifetime, turbulence and colour behaviour.
copy.interaction: Adjust any control. The effect in the chamber reshapes immediately — there is no apply step.
copy.explore: The chamber is transparent on all sides. The same effect reads differently from each.

projects.name: Parable
projects.summary: A gesture-first god-game where miracles are drawn rather than selected from a menu.
projects.brief: Parable is a browser god-game in which the player's input is gesture: miracles are performed by drawing them, and the simulation responds. The core loop centres on a single well-developed miracle rather than a broad ability list, and ritual interactions build on top of it.
projects.lesson: One deeply implemented verb produces more play than six shallow ones.

projects.name: Starlight Acre
projects.summary: Farming in orbit, where the greenhouse is failing and every resource is a shared constraint.
projects.brief: Starlight Acre is a Godot farming game set on an orbital station whose greenhouse is failing. Power, water and nutrients are shared, finite and interdependent, so growing mythic crops is a scheduling problem as much as a cultivation one, assisted by a gardener drone.
projects.lesson: Coupling resources that players expect to be independent is a cheap way to create real decisions.

copy.subtitle: Two Verbs
copy.plaque: One deeply implemented verb produces more play than six shallow ones.
copy.problem: Two games, opposite in temperament: one about intervention, one about patience.
copy.made: A gesture-first browser god-game built around a single well-developed miracle, and an orbital farming game where power, water and nutrients are one coupled system.
copy.interaction: One side of the portal offers a branching decision. The other lets you plant something and wait for it.
copy.explore: The installation is one object with two faces. Neither side can see the other.

projects.name: S'mores Katamari
projects.summary: A rolling collection game set in a compressed model of a real town, starring Smudge.
projects.brief: S'mores Katamari is a Three.js game in the Katamari idiom: roll, collect, grow. Its playspace is a compressed version of a real Vancouver Island town, laid out with reference to actual map data, and it runs entirely offline once loaded.
projects.lesson: Real geography makes a good starting point and a bad final layout; the editing is the design work.

copy.subtitle: A Real Town, Compressed
copy.plaque: Real geography is a good starting point and a bad final layout. The editing is the design work.
copy.problem: Actual distances are boring at play speed, but a town that loses its shape stops being recognisable.
copy.made: A rolling collection game set in a compressed model of a real Vancouver Island town, laid out against real map data and running fully offline.
copy.interaction: Take control of the ball. Roll, collect, and grow — one short self-contained level.
copy.explore: The diorama is a miniature neighbourhood. Everything in it is collectible at sufficient size.

projects.name: Endless Grok / Void Ascendancy
projects.summary: A complete browser 4X: deterministic galaxies, AI empires, research, diplomacy, crises and saves.
projects.brief: Endless Grok is a playable 4X space strategy game running in the browser, with deterministic galaxy generation, multiple factions, AI empires, economy, research, diplomacy, combat, crisis events, save support and a long tail of enhancement work.
projects.lesson: Deterministic world generation is a testing feature first and a player feature second.

copy.subtitle: A 4X in a Browser Tab
copy.plaque: Deterministic world generation is a testing feature first and a player feature second.
copy.problem: Strategy games plateau in the mid-game, and their AI opponents become unreadable.
copy.made: A complete browser 4X with deterministic galaxy generation, factions, AI empires, economy, research, diplomacy, combat, crises and saves.
copy.interaction: Claim nodes on the galactic board, choose one technology, and watch the expansion consequences resolve.
copy.explore: The same seed always produces the same galaxy. Reset the board and it returns identical.

projects.name: Big Mac Westcat SSH
projects.summary: The governed access route between a laptop and the machine that does the heavy work.
projects.brief: This project is the access layer of the local AI infrastructure: a single canonical, key-authenticated route from the portable machine to the compute host's service account, with explicit boundaries about what that account may do. It is small, unglamorous, and everything else in this wing depends on it.
projects.lesson: Infrastructure that is not written down becomes infrastructure nobody is willing to change.

projects.name: BigMac Storage and SMB
projects.summary: Large local volumes shared across a private network and deliberately never exposed to the internet.
projects.brief: Directly attached storage on the compute host is shared over the local network and a private mesh network to a small number of known devices. The defining constraint is negative: this storage has no public route, no cloud tier and no external synchronisation.
projects.lesson: For large private data, the cheapest security control is having no public route at all.

projects.name: BigMac Ollama + Codex Integration
projects.summary: A development tool on the laptop using models that are actually running on another machine.
projects.brief: This integration lets a coding assistant on the portable machine call a local model server on the compute host through an encrypted tunnel, using a dedicated provider profile and launcher configuration. To the tool, the model is local. To the network, nothing is exposed.
projects.lesson: A tunnel that makes a remote service look local is often simpler than teaching a tool that remote services exist.

projects.name: Hermes Agent/Desktop + BigMac
projects.summary: A desktop control surface for an agent gateway whose engine lives on the compute host.
projects.brief: Hermes provides an agent gateway and interface; the arrangement here keeps that interface on the laptop and its inference engine on the compute host, connected by a tunnel. It is the same split the rest of this wing uses — control here, computation there.
projects.lesson: Separating control surface from compute lets each run where it is actually good.

projects.name: Large Language Launcher
projects.summary: A launcher that turns a scattered collection of local AI tools into a single card-based menu.
projects.brief: Local AI tooling accumulates as a heap of scripts, environments and start commands. The Large Language Launcher presents them as a manifest-backed set of cards, each knowing how to start its own tool, so the collection becomes navigable instead of remembered.
projects.lesson: Personal infrastructure needs a table of contents before it needs more features.

projects.name: project_daemon / DAEMON
projects.summary: A persistent digital lifeform on a home network, with circadian behaviour, drift, and real permanent death.
projects.brief: DAEMON runs continuously rather than being invoked. It has a soul file defining its identity, persistent memory in a local database and vector store, a circadian rhythm, behavioural drift over time, telemetry, hibernation, a sanctuary state — and genuine permadeath, with a graveyard for instances that have ended.
projects.lesson: Continuity only means something where ending is possible.

copy.subtitle: The Machinery Behind the Work
copy.plaque: Six infrastructure projects that decide which machine does the work — and where nothing is permitted to go.
copy.problem: Local AI work needs real compute, large private storage and a trustworthy path between machines.
copy.made: A governed access route, a private storage architecture with no public path, a tunnelled local inference integration, an agent control surface, a launcher for the resulting tool sprawl, and a persistent daemon with real permadeath.
copy.interaction: Select a workflow. A pulse travels the sculpture through the exact nodes that workflow touches.
copy.explore: Every address, hostname and identifier in this room is a synthetic example. No credential, key or operational configuration appears anywhere in this museum.

projects.name: Big Mac FaceTools
projects.summary: A face-processing stack kept entirely on one machine, with no network path off it.
projects.brief: FaceTools runs face detection, analysis and transformation locally on the compute host, controlled from the laptop. Models and data live on external roots outside the application, and the stack has no outbound network path — a boundary chosen because of what the data is.
projects.lesson: Some data categories decide the architecture before any engineering discussion starts.

projects.name: OSINT Box
projects.summary: An open-source research platform that runs locally, so investigations leave no trail with a service provider.
projects.brief: OSINT Box is a fully local research platform: a Python service, a tactical web interface, a native wrapper, case and result storage, local model integration, streaming jobs and a set of research tools. Running locally means the investigation itself is not disclosed to any third party.
projects.lesson: For research tooling, where the query is logged matters as much as what the tool can find.

copy.subtitle: The Trust Boundary
copy.plaque: Some data categories decide the architecture before any engineering discussion begins.
copy.problem: Face processing and open-source research both generate exactly the material you least want logged elsewhere.
copy.made: A local-only face-processing stack with no outbound network path, and a fully local research platform where the investigation is never disclosed to a service provider.
copy.interaction: Run the face bay on synthetic generated faces; run the research bay on a fictional investigation. The wall between the bays shows what does not cross it.
copy.explore: The trust-boundary wall is a physical object here because it is the architectural decision both projects are built on.
